Reproductive ecology of the Slabrock darter (Etheostoma smithi) has been examined through field collections in the Duck River system, where mature females attain a maximum adult body mass of approximately 1.58 grams [Wwi = approximately 1.58 grams], reflecting the energetic equilibrium achieved in a small-stream environment with seasonally variable food availability. This modest size places the species among the smaller members of the genus Etheostoma, and comparisons with related darters suggest that this ultimate body mass is achieved relatively early in life. Field surveys indicate that the total length at puberty, estimated from histological examination of gonadal tissue combined with length-frequency data, is 2.98 cm [Lp = 2.98 cm]. This value suggests that individuals begin investing in reproductive structures well before reaching somatic maturity, a pattern observed in several benthic-stream fishes that face variable adult mortality regimes. The wet weight at birth, calculated using the measured egg diameter of 2.2 mm and the formula for a prolate spheroid, is approximately 0.0056 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.0056 grams]. This small initial mass is typical of darters that produce relatively large, yolky eggs. Collectively, these data provide a comprehensive baseline for understanding the life-history strategy of this species.

Embryonic development in this species proceeds at a rapid pace under controlled thermal conditions. Eggs incubated at a stable temperature of 21 °C [T = 21 °C] typically complete eclosion after 13 days, with the prolarvae then entering a brief yolk-sac stage. The age at birth, defined here as the point at which the yolk-sac larva is free and begins to exhibit active swimming and mouth opening, is approximately 21 days [ab = approximately 21 days], a duration consistent with that reported for other small darters of the subgenus Ulocentra, although slight variation may occur depending on local t at a temperature of 21 °C [T = 21 °C]hermal regimes. Following the absorption of the yolk, the free-swimming larva must locate suitable prey quickly, and this transition represents a critical bottleneck in early life history. The presence of sufficient microcrustacean prey in the natal riffle is likely essential for survival during this vulnerable window.

Longevity data from mark-recapture studies conducted in the Buffalo River watershed indicate that Slabrock darter maximum lifespan is approximately 730 days [am = approximately 730 days] under natural thermal conditions averaging 18 °C [T = 18 °C]. This relatively short lifespan, typical of many small-bodied stream fishes, constrains the species to a single or perhaps two reproductive seasons. The data suggest that most individuals spawn during their first spring following maturation, with very few surviving to a second breeding season. These demographic constraints place a premium on early maturity and efficient investment in reproductive effort. The 730-day figure is derived from direct observations of tagged individuals and represents the maximum recorded interval between initial capture and final recapture, making it a robust estimate of field longevity. Given the high mortality rates typical of small benthic fishes, the realized mean lifespan is likely substantially shorter.

The total length of mature individuals provides a useful metric for assessing population structure and growth performance. The ultimate total length for Slabrock darter, based on measurements of the largest individuals encountered during multiple sampling seasons, is 6.2 cm [Li = 6.2 cm]. This size is modest relative to many other darters, though it is consistent with the species' preferred habitat of shallow, gravel-bottomed riffles where body size may be constrained by interstitial space and flow regime. Growth appears to slow considerably after the first year, with most length accretion occurring during the initial growing season. The relationship between length and mass follows the standard power function observed in many fishes, and the derived adult body mass of 1.58 g [Wwi = 1.58 g] aligns well with expectations for a fish of this length. Comparative data from sympatric congeners suggest that this growth trajectory is adapted to the productivity of the small-stream environment.

Gonadal development and the timing of reproductive events are tightly coupled with seasonal temperature cycles in this species. Histological analyses confirm that females become gravid in early spring, with peak spawning activity coinciding with moderate water temperatures. The age at first reproduction, which closely follows the attainment of the 2.98 cm [Lp = 2.98 cm] length at puberty, is likely achieved within the first year of life for most individuals. Spawning appears to occur over a relatively compressed interval, and females deposit their adhesive eggs within interstitial spaces of gravel substrate. The total length of 6.2 cm [Li = 6.2 cm] represents the upper bound of somatic growth, and few individuals exceed this threshold given the constraints of the 730-day lifespan (730 days) [am = 730 days] observed under field conditions at an average water temperature of 18 °C [T = 18 °C]. The species thus exhibits a classic fast life-history strategy, prioritizing early reproduction over extended growth.
